blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Dear children,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have seen in previous classes how measurements are
converted to numbers and how problems about measurements
are solved by converting them to number problems and then to
algebraic problems. Thus we came to understand how relations
between operations on pure numbers develop into algebraic
principles, which in turn are used to solve problems about
measurements. We also saw how special properties of various
figures are turned into geometrical theorems.

In this textbook, we move a little more into these various
avenues of mathematics. Here we get the first glimpses of
how the usually separate disciplines of algebra and geometry
merge into a new branch of mathematics. The basic ideas of
probability theory, which is used in all sciences and which is an
essential component of artificial intelligence used widely now.

The fundamental ideas needed for those who opt for
mathematics as a part of their continuing education are all
discussed in our textbooks. The inherent value of these
books is the culture of mathematical thinking which everyone
should be able to acquire as they finish one stage of their
basic education. The essence of this culture is the ability
to analyze everything logically and form conclusions
based only on such reflection

We have been talking about the products of the parts of two intersecting chords in a

Some chords pass through a single point within the circle. The point divides each chord

other point on the line divides into parts of different lengths. We use ratios to specify

Slope and perpendicularity

It is not difficult to see that the slopes of parallel
lines are equal. What is the relation between the
slopes of perpendicular lines?

Suppose that lines of slopes $p$ and $q$ are perpendicular
to each other. Let's take their point of intersection
as $(a, b)$.

Then the point $(a + 1, b + p)$ is on the first line and
the point $(a + 1, b + q)$ is on the second line (why?)

Since the lines are perpendicular, the points $(a, b)$,
$(a + 1, b + p)$, $(a + 1, b + q)$ are the vertices of
a right-angled triangle. The hypotenuse is the line
joining the second and third points. So, the squares
of the lengths of the perpendicular sides of this
triangle are $p^2 + 1$ and $q^2 + 1$ and the length of the
hypotenuse is $|p - q|$.

This gives $(p^2 + 1) + (q^2 + 1) = (p - q)^2$

Simplifying, this gives

$$2 = -2pq$$

which means

$$pq = -1$$

Thus, for lines perpendicular to each other, the slope
of one is the negative of the reciprocal of the other.

Class 9? How did we draw the graph of the
polynomial $p(x) = 2x + 1$?
That method can now be described like this:
Took several numbers as $x$ and calculated
$2x + 1$ for each of these.
Marked those points with these pairs of
numbers as coordinates and joined them.
Thus the equation of the line drawn is

$$y = 2x + 1$$

In general, the graph of the first degree
polynomial

$$p(x) = ax + b$$

is the line whose equation is

$$y = ax + b$$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Equation of a circle

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We can join any two points to draw a line. And if we know the coordinates of these
points, we can find the equation of the line also; that is the algebraic form of the relation
between the coordinates of any point on the line.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Like this, if we fix a point and a number, we can draw a circle with the point as centre
and the number as radius. If we know the coordinates of the centre and the number
which is the radius, can we find the relation between the coordinates of every point on
the circle?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For example, let’s look at the circle with centre $(1, 4)$ and radius $2$. For any point on this
circle, the distance from the centre is $2$:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have seen that the square of the distance between the points $(1, 4)$ and $(x, y)$ is
$$(x - 1)^2 + (y - 4)^2.$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: If $(x, y)$ is a point on the circle, then this square is $2^2 = 4$. That is,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus the coordinates of any point on the circle satisfies this equation. On the other hand,
if any pair $x, y$ of numbers satisfy this equation, then the point with these as coordinates
is at a distance $\sqrt{4} = 2$ from the point $(1, 4)$ and so it is a point on the circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Thus this is the equation of the circle with centre $(1, 4)$ and radius $2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We can also expand this and write

$$x^2 + y^2 - 2x - 8y + 13 = 0$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, what is the equation of the circle with centre at the origin and radius 1?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If we take the coordinates of a point on this circle as $(x, y)$, the square of the distance
from the origin to this, which is $x^2 + y^2$ must be equal to the square of the radius, which
is 1. So, the equation of this circle is

$$x^2 + y^2 = 1$$

A square in the middle and four triangles around it; all four of them are isosceles triangles

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
What shape is this? Can't be called a prism;
prisms have two equal bases and rectangles on the
sides. In the shape we have made now, we have a
square at the bottom, a point on top and triangles

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Instead of a square, the base can be some other
rectangle, a triangle or some other polygon. Try! (It is better looking when the base is a
regular polygon).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Such a solid is generally called a pyramid.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The sides of the polygon forming the base of a pyramid
are called **base edges** and the other sides of the triangles
are called **lateral edges**. The topmost point of a pyramid
is called its **apex**.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The height of a prism is the distance between its bases,
isn't it? The height of a pyramid is the perpendicular
distance from the apex to the base.

blocks.label: Section-title

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
What is the surface area of a square pyramid of base edges 10 centimetres and lateral
edges 13 centimetres? The surface area is the area of paper needed to make it. How will
it look if we cut this pyramid open and lay it flat?

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The area of the square is easily seen to be 100 square centimetres. What about the
triangles?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The area of the triangle is half the product of its base and height, isn't
it?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For that, we need the height of the triangle. Since the triangle is
isosceles, this altitude bisects the base.

So using Pythagoras Theorem, the height of the triangle is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = 12 \text{ centimetres} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Thus the area of the triangle is $5 \times 12 = 60$ square centimetres.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
What will be the height of the triangle when the paper is
turned into a pyramid?

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:

height

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This length is called the slant height of the pyramid.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have seen the relation between the base
edge, lateral edge and slant height of a
pyramid in the problem we did just now. As
shown in the picture on the right, there is a
right triangle on each side of the pyramid -
its perpendicular sides are the slant height
and half the base edge, the hypotenuse is a
lateral edge.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now do this problem: what is the surface
area of a square pyramid with base edges 2
metres and lateral edges 3 metres?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The base area is 4 square metres. To compute
the areas of lateral faces, we need the slant
height. In the right triangle mentioned
above, one side is half the base edge, that
is, 1 metre and the hypotenuse is the lateral
edge of 3 metres.

So, the slant height is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \sqrt{3^2 - 1^2} = 2\sqrt{2} \text{ metres} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Using this, the area of each triangular face is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 2\sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2} \text{ square metres.} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the surface area of the pyramid is

$$4 + (4 \times 2\sqrt{2}) = 4 + 8\sqrt{2} \text{ square metres.}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If not satisfied with this, a calculator can be used, (or an approximate value of $\sqrt{2}$
recalled) to compute this as 15.31 square metres.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have seen that the volume of any prism is equal
to the product of the base area and the height. What
about the volume of a pyramid?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let's take the case of a square pyramid. Make a
hollow square pyramid with thick paper and also a
square prism of the same base and height.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Fill the pyramid with sand and transfer it to the
prism. Measure the height of the sand in the prism and
see what fraction of the height of the prism it is. A third,
isn’t it? So to fill the prism, how many times should we
fill the pyramid?

blocks.text:
Thus we see that the volume of the prism is three times
the volume of the pyramid. (A mathematical explanation
of this is given at the end of this lesson).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have seen in Class 9 that the volume of a prism is
equal to the product of the base area and the height.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So what can we say about the volume of a square
pyramid?

blocks.label: Paragraph

centimetres is $\frac{1}{3} \times 10^2 \times 8 = 266\frac{2}{3}$ cubic centimetres.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A metal cube of edge 15 centimetres is melted and recast into a square pyramid of base

blocks.label: Paragraph

Since the base area of our pyramid is $25^2$ square centimetres, a third of the height is
$\frac{15^3}{25^2}$ and so the height is,

$$ 3 \times \frac{15^3}{25^2} = 16.2 \text{ centimetres.} $$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Cone

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Cylinders are prism-like solids with circular bases. Similarly, we have pyramid-like
solids with circular bases:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
They are called cones.

We can make a cylinder by rolling up a rectangle. Likewise, we can make a cone by
rolling up a sector of a circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
What is the relation between the dimensions of the sector we start with and the cone we
end up with?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The radius of the sector becomes the slant height of the cone.
The arc length of the sector becomes the circumference of the
base of the cone.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Cone
We can draw
cones in GeoGebra, just
as we drew pyramids.
Draw a circle in Graphics
and in 3D Graphics,
use Extrude to Pyramid
or Cone. The base
radius and height can be
changed using sliders.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We often specify the size of a sector in terms of the central angle. See this problem:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From a circle of radius 12 centimetres, a sector of central angle $45^{\circ}$ is cut out and
made into a cone. What are the slant height and base radius of this cone?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The slant height of the cone is the radius of the circle itself: 12 centimetres. What about
its base radius?

$45^{\circ}$ is $\frac{1}{8}$ of $360^{\circ}$. And the arc length of a sector is proportional to the central angle. So
this arc length is $\frac{1}{8}$ of the circumference of the full circle.

This arc becomes the base circle of the cone. Thus the circumference of the base circle of
the cone is $\frac{1}{8}$ of the circumference of the larger circle from which the sector was cut out.
Since radii of circles are proportional to their circumferences, the radius of the smaller
circle is $\frac{1}{8}$ of the radius of the large circle. Thus the radius of the base of the cone is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{1}{8} \times 12 = 1.5 \text{ centimetres.} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: How about a question in the reverse direction?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: How do we make a cone of base radius 5 centimetres and slant height 15 centimetres?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To make a cone, we need a sector. Since the slant height is to be 15 centimetres, the
sector must be cut out from a circle of radius 15 centimetres.

What should be its central angle?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The radius of the small circle forming the base of the cone is $\frac{5}{15} = \frac{1}{3}$ of the radius of
the large circle from which the sector is to be cut out. (How do we get this?) So, the
circumference of the small circle is also $\frac{1}{3}$ of the circumference of the large circle.

The circumference of the small circle is the arc length of the sector. Thus the arc of
the sector is $\frac{1}{3}$ of the circle from which it is cut out. So its central angle must be
$360^{\circ} \times \frac{1}{3} = 120^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Curved surface area

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As in the case of a cylinder, a cone also has a curved surface - the part which rises up
at a slant. The area of this curved surface is the area of the sector used to make the cone.
(For a cylinder also, the area of the curved surface is the area of the rectangle rolled up
to make it, isn't it?)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: See this problem:

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
For a cone drawn in
GeoGebra, the curved
surface area can be seen
under Surface in the Algebra
window.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To make a conical hat of base radius 8 centimetres and
slant height 30 centimetres, how much square centimetres
of paper do we need?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
What we need here is the area of the sector we roll up to make this hat. Since the slant
height is to be 30 centimetres, we must cut out the sector from a circle of this radius.
Also the radius of the small circle forming the base of the cone must be 8 centimetres,
that is $\frac{8}{30} = \frac{4}{15}$ of the radius of the large circle from which the sector is cut out. So the
circumference of the small circle is also the same fraction of the circumference of the
large circle. The arc length of the sector is the circumference of the small circle. Thus
the sector to be cut out is $\frac{4}{15}$ of the full circle. So, its area is that fraction of the area of
the circle; that is,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\pi \times 30^2 \times \frac{4}{15} = \pi \times 2 \times 30 \times 4 = 240\pi$ square centimetres.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus we need $240\pi$ square centimetres of paper to make the hat (it can be computed as
approximately 754 square centimetres).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As in a pyramid, the height of a cone is the
perpendicular distance from the apex to the base,
and it is the distance between the apex and the centre
of the base circle.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Curved surface

The area of the curved surface of a cone
is the area of the sector used to make it.
If we take the base radius of the cone as
$r$ and its slant height as $l$, then the radius
of the sector is $l$ and its central angle is
$\frac{r}{l} \times 360^{\circ}$. So its area is
$$\frac{1}{360} \times \left(\frac{r}{l} \times 360\right) \times \pi l^2 = \pi r l$$
(Recall the computation of the area of a
sector in Class 9).

Thus the area of the curved surface of
a cone is half the product of the base
circumference and the slant height.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Again, as in the case of a square pyramid, the height is
related to the slant height via a right triangle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For example, in a cone of base radius 5 centimetres and
height 10 centimetres the slant height is

$$\sqrt{5^2 + 10^2} = \sqrt{125} = 5\sqrt{5} \text{ centimetres.}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To find the volume of a cone, we can do an experiment
similar to the one we did to find the volume of a square
pyramid. Make a cone and a cylinder of the same base
and height. Fill the cone with sand and transfer it to the
cylinder. Here also, we can see that the volume of the cone
is a third of the volume of the cylinder. Thus we have the
following:

draw a cylinder and

blocks.label: Paragraph

For example, the volume of a cone of base radius 4 centimetres and height 6 centimetres
is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 4^2 \times 6 = 32\pi \text{ cubic centimetres.} $$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Sphere

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Round solids enter our lives in various
ways - as the thrill of ball games and as the
sweetness of laddus. Now let’s look at the
mathematics of such solids called **spheres**.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If we slice a cylinder or cone parallel to a
base, we get a circle. In whatever way we slice a sphere, we get a circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The distance of any point on a circle from the centre is the same. A sphere also has a
$centre$, from which the distance to any point on its surface is the same. This distance
is called the $radius$ of the sphere and double this is called the
$diameter$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If we slice a sphere into exact halves, we get a circle whose
centre, radius and diameter are those of the sphere itself.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We cannot cut open a sphere and spread it flat, as we did with
other solids. The fact is that we cannot make the surface of a
sphere flat without some folding or stretching.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
But we can prove that the surface area of a sphere of radius $r$ is $4\pi r^2$ (an explanation is
given at the end of the lesson).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We can state this in a different way.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text: The surface area of a sphere is equal to the square of its radius multiplied by $4\pi$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Also, we can prove that the volume of a sphere of radius $r$ is $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ (An explanation of
this also is given at the end of the lesson).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: See this problem:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
What is the surface area of the largest sphere that
can be carved from a cube of edge 8 centimetres?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We can see from the picture that the diameter of the
sphere is the length of an edge of the cube. So, the
surface area of the sphere is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $4\pi \times 4^2 = 64\pi$ square centimetres

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Sphere and cylinder

Consider a cylinder which can cover a
sphere precisely. Its base radius is the
radius of the sphere and its height is
double its radius.

So if we take the radius
of the sphere as $r$, the
base radius and height
of the cylinder are $r$
and $2r$. So its surface
area is

$$(2\pi r \times 2r) + (2 \times \pi r^2) = 6\pi r^2$$

The surface area of the sphere is $4\pi r^2$.
Thus the ratio of these surface areas is
$3 : 2$.

Again, the volume of the cylinder is

$$\pi r^2 \times 2r = 2\pi r^3$$

and the volume of the sphere is $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, so
that the ratio of the volumes is also $3 : 2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Another problem:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A solid sphere of radius 12 centimetres is cut into
two equal halves. What is the surface area of each
hemisphere?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The surface of the hemisphere consists of half the surface of
the sphere and a circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Since the radius of the sphere is 12 centimetres, its area is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $4\pi \times 12^2 = 576\pi$ square centimetres

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since the radius of the circle is 12 centimetres, its area is

The surface area of the hemisphere is half of this added to the area of the circle.

$\pi \times 12^2 = 144\pi$ square centimetres

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So the surface area of the hemisphere is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\frac{1}{2} \times 576\pi + 144\pi = 432\pi$ square centimetres

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have seen only the techniques of calculating volumes of pyramids and cones, and
also the surface area and volume of a sphere. For those who may be interested in knowing
how they are actually got, we give some explanations below.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Volume of a pyramid

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We can think of a stack of square plates, of decreasing
size as an approximation to a square pyramid.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As we decrease the thickness of the plates and
increase their number, we get better approximations.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: And the sum of the volumes of these plates gets nearer to the volume of the pyramid.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Suppose we use 10 plates, to start with. Each plate is a square prism of small height.
Let's use plates of the same height. So, if we take the height of the pyramid as $h$, each
plate is of height $\frac{1}{10}h$. How do we compute the base
of each plate?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If we imagine the pyramid and the stack of plates
sliced vertically down from the vertex, we get a
picture like this.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Starting from the top, we have isosceles triangles of
increasing size. Their heights increase at the rate of
$\frac{1}{10}h$ for each plate.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since these triangles are all similar (why?) their bases also increase at the same rate. So,
if we take the base edge of the bases of the pyramid to be $b$, the bases of the triangles
starting from the top are $\frac{1}{10}b, \frac{2}{10}b, ..., b$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the volumes of the plates are

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \left( \frac{1}{10} b \right)^2 \times \frac{1}{10} h, \left( \frac{2}{10} b \right)^2 \times \frac{1}{10} h, ..., b^2 \times \frac{1}{10} h $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: And their sum?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have seen how such sums can be computed in the section, Sum of Squares of the
lesson Arithmetic Sequences.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Thus the sum of the volumes

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{1}{1000} b^2 h \times \frac{1}{6} \times 10 \times 11 \times 21 = \frac{1}{6} b^2 h \times \frac{10}{10} \times \frac{11}{10} \times \frac{21}{10} = \frac{1}{6} b^2 h \times 1.1 \times 2.1 $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now imagine 100 such plates (we cannot draw it anyway).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The thickness of a plate becomes $\frac{1}{100}h$ and the base edges would be $\frac{1}{100}b, \frac{2}{100}b, \frac{3}{100}b, ..., b.$
So the sum of the volumes would be

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
What if we increase the number of plates to $1000$? Without going through detailed
computations, we can see that the sum of volumes would be

$$ \frac{1}{6} b^2 h \times 1.001 \times 2.001 $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: What is the number to which these sums get closer and closer to?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: It is the volume of the pyramid; and it is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{1}{6} b^2 h \times 1 \times 2 = \frac{1}{3} b^2 h $$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Volume of a cone

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Just as we stacked square plates to
approximate a pyramid, we can stack
circular plates to approximate a cone.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
And in much the same way, we can
compute the volume of a cone also.

What is the relation between the dimensions of the
small and large cones?

blocks.label: Paragraph

If we take the base radius, height and slant height

blocks.label: Equation

To compute the area of the curved surface of these frustums, let's consider one of these.
Let's take its height as $h$ and the radius of its middle circle as $m$. Let's also take the radius

The area of the curved surface of the frustum

last page. And this is equal to $2\pi rh$, by
the above equation; that is, the area of the

and height $h$.

So what do we get? In the solid which
approximates the sphere, the curved surface
area of each frustum is equal to that of a
cylinder of the same height with base radius
equal to that of the sphere.

So the curved surface area of the whole
approximating solid is equal to the sum of the
curved surface areas of all these cylinders.
And what do we get on putting together
all these cylinders? A large cylinder, just
covering the sphere.

If we cut off a small cone from the top of a cone,

How do we find the area of the curved surface of a
frustum in terms of its slant height and base radii?

Taking the slant heights of the large and small

$$= \pi(r + R)d$$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Not a correct average

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: The monthly income of 10 households in a neighbourhood are these:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: What is the mean monthly income?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Adding all these and dividing by 10, we get the mean monthly income as 19285 rupees.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, if instead of taking all these incomes separately, we had only the mean, then also
we can make some conclusions about the general economic status of the households:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\bullet$ The monthly income of all these households are around 19285 rupees.

$\bullet$ None of the households has a monthly income very much greater or very much less
than 19285 rupees.

$\bullet$ The number of households with monthly income greater than 19285 rupees is more
or less equal to the number of households with monthly income less than 19285
rupees.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now suppose someone with a monthly income of 175000 rupees comes to live in the
neighbourhood. What is the mean monthly income of the 11 households?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Without giving all these details, if this mean only is given, wouldn’t we make the wrong
conclusion that all these households have a monthly income around 30000 rupees? This
is almost one and a half times the monthly income of ten of these households.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The purpose of calculating the mean is to reduce a whole collection of numbers to a
single number, which gives a general understanding of a situation. But numbers in the
collection which are very much less or very much more than others (though few) affect
the mean a lot.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In our example, it was a single number very much larger than the first ten which changed
the mean so much. Can you think of other instances like this where very small or very
large numbers influence the mean to give a wrong impression?

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Another average

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let's see how we can compute another average which gives a better overall indication of
the monthly income of the 11 households. If we write all the incomes in increasing order
and take the middle number, 5 of the households would have income less than this and
5 of them would have more.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let's write the numbers in order:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The middle number is 19500. It is called the $median$ of these numbers. That is, the
median monthly income of the 11 households is 19500 rupees. We can put it like this:
of all the 11 households, 5 have monthly income less than 19500 rupees and 5 have more
than 19500 rupees. That is, the number of households with income less than the median
and the number of households with income more than the median are equal.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
What if we take only the first 10 households? If we write incomes in the increasing
order, there would be two numbers, 18600 and 19500 at the middle, instead of just one
number.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here also, we must choose the median such that the number of items below it and above
it are equal. Any number between 18600 and 19500 would do for this. Usually half their
sum is taken as the median.

That is, the median monthly income of the first 10 households is

$$ \frac{1}{2}(18600 + 19500) = 19050 \text{ rupees} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The median income 19050 rupees, like the mean income 19285 rupees gives a reasonable
estimate of the economic status of the first ten households (and there is no great difference
between the mean and the median either).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
What is important here is that the high income of the eleventh household does not change
the median much. Also if we say that the median income of some households is 19050

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
rupees and that the monthly income of one of these is 21000 rupees, we can conclude
that this household is better off than more than half the households considered.

$\bullet$ The daily wage of the $14^{\text{th}}$ worker is $605$ rupees.

$\bullet$ The daily wage of each one thereafter, till the $23^{\text{rd}}$ increases by $10$ rupees.

$\bullet$ To reach the $21^{\text{st}}$ worker we want, from the $14^{\text{th}}$, we must take $7$ more workers.

blocks.text: Now it is an arithmetic problem, isn't it?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:

blocks.label: Paragraph

As in the previous problem, we divide the 5 years between 40 and 45 into 10 equal parts,
and assume that each such subdivision contains one person whose age is the midvalue
of his class.

Then each subdivision is $\frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2}$ year. The age of the $20^{\text{th}}$ person is the midvalue of

increases by $\frac{1}{2}$ year (till the $29^{\text{th}}$). So the age of the $23^{\text{rd}}$ person is

blocks.text: $$40\frac{1}{4} + \left(3 \times \frac{1}{2}\right) = 40\frac{1}{4} + 1\frac{1}{2} = 41\frac{3}{4} \text{ years}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Dear Children,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Wouldn’t you like to know about your rights? Awareness about your rights will inspire
and motivate you to ensure your protection and participation, thereby making social
justice a reality. You may know that a commission for child rights is functioning in our
state called the **Kerala State Commission for Protection of Child Rights.**

Let's see what your rights are:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
• Right to freedom of speech and
expression.

• Right to life and liberty.

• Right to maximum survival and
development.

• Right to be respected and accepted
regardless of caste, creed and colour.

• Right to protection and care against
physical, mental and sexual abuse.

• Right to participation.

• Protection from child labour and
hazardous work.

• Protection against child marriage.

• Right to know one’s culture and live
accordingly.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
• Protection against neglect.

• Right to free and compulsory
education.

• Right to learn, rest and leisure.

• Right to parental and societal care,
and protection.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Major Responsibilities

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
• Protect school and public facilities.
• Observe punctuality in learning
and activities of the school.
• Accept and respect school
authorities, teachers, parents and
fellow students.
• Readiness to accept and respect
others regardless of caste, creed or
colour.
